solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Kind of pie mainly containing sheep’s smoked meat (8)

indicatorNotes.mainly: 'mainly' means for the most part, so most of the word stays and its last letter goes
indicatorNotes.containing: the shortened pie holds the sheep inside it, as a container holds its contents

blocks.note: PASTIE, a spelling of pasty, without its last letter
a ram is a male sheep; the 's stands for 'is'

annotation.surface: A deli order: a pie stuffed mostly with smoked mutton.
annotation.walkthrough: A pastie is a pasty, the Cornish folded meat pie. 'Sheep’s' reads as a possessive attached to the meat, but it is 'sheep is', which frees smoked meat to be the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Pastrami is a plain example of the class: beef that is brined, spiced and then smoked.

entries.clue: Father with length in fabric (6)

annotation.surface: Dad is measured up inside a bolt of cloth.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction putting L inside something, but it is simply the last two letters, written as printed.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: poplin is one particular fabric, a plain-woven cotton used for shirts.

entries.clue: Succulent seed produce (9)

blocks.note: the stone of a plum or cherry is its seed

annotation.surface: A description of juicy seeds and fruit from the garden.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Succulent' reads as an adjective for the produce, but it is the noun: a plant with fleshy, water-storing leaves.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: stonecrop, or sedum, is one of the succulent plants that grow on walls and rocks.

entries.clue: Wild Brazilian city according to the Times? (7)

blocks.note: 'to us' = in our view, where 'us' is the Times talking about itself

annotation.surface: A newspaper's verdict on how wild Rio is.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue appears in the Times, so the paper can speak of itself as 'us'; the question mark flags that self-reference.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a riotous party is a wild, unrestrained one.

entries.clue: Anger suppressed by doctor unable to move easily (5)

indicatorNotes.suppressed by: to suppress anger is to hold it down inside you, so the doctor keeps IRE inside

annotation.surface: A doctor bottling up rage, stiff and slow-moving.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface runs straight on from doctor to 'unable to move easily', as if describing the doctor; the definition starts at 'unable'.
annotation.definitionFit: Mired is literally stuck in a mire, a bog, where every step is a struggle.

entries.clue: Heading for Italy, opera-singer stopping short, victim of flight problems (6)

indicatorNotes.Heading for: the heading of a word is its top, its first letter
indicatorNotes.stopping short: the singer's name stops before it is finished, losing its last letter

blocks.note: CARUSO, the Italian tenor, without the O

annotation.surface: A travel mishap: an opera singer bound for Italy whose trip is cut short.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a delayed flight; the real flight problem is Greek myth, wax wings melting near the sun.
annotation.definitionFit: Icarus flew too close to the sun, his wings failed and he fell into the sea: a literal flight problem.

entries.clue: Opening of cut on shepherd’s shin? (7)

indicatorNotes.Opening of: the opening of a word is where it begins, its first letter

blocks.note: one who lambs, delivering lambs; the 's is 'is'

annotation.surface: A shepherd with a cut on the shin.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shin' looks like part of the leg, but it is the verb, as in shinning up a tree. The question mark owns up to LAMBER as a rare word for a shepherd.
annotation.definitionFit: Shin and clamber are both verbs for climbing awkwardly using hands and legs.

entries.clue: Regular character in SF book entering base (5)

indicatorNotes.entering: the book goes into the base as a person enters a room

blocks.note: a root is a base or foundation

annotation.surface: A reader spotting a recurring character in a science-fiction novel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'SF book' looks like one phrase, but the definition stops at SF and 'book' starts the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: robots are one of science fiction's stock figures.

entries.clue: No specific group to bridge river in county (8)

indicatorNotes.to bridge: a bridge spans a gap, so the river sits in the gap between the two pieces

blocks.note: 'some' = an unspecified one, as in 'some person'

annotation.surface: An unnamed group plans to build a bridge over a river in the county.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface has a group building a bridge over the river; in the letters the river is the bridge, spanning the gap between the other two words.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Somerset is a county in south-west England.

entries.clue: Wise to limit medicine waste (8)

indicatorNotes.to limit: a limit hems something in, so SAGE closes around the medicine

blocks.note: a pill is a dose of medicine

annotation.surface: Sensible advice to cut down on wasted medicine.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one piece of advice; 'medicine waste' splits, with 'waste' alone the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Spillage is material lost by spilling, one kind of waste.

entries.clue: Where you might be expected to keep still? (10,5)

annotation.definition: Where you might be expected to keep still?

blocks.note: the surface reading: stay motionless, as a photographer tells a sitter
the meant reading: a still is a photograph, and this is where you keep stills

annotation.surface: A sitter told to hold still for a portrait.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Keep still' reads as 'don't move', the photographer's order; read it as 'keep stills', store your snapshots.
annotation.definitionFit: Stills are photographs, and the album is the book that stores them; the clue's 'where' asks for a place of keeping.

entries.clue: Dispassionate cricketing body in the past welcomes conclusion of game (3-4)

indicatorNotes.welcomes: to welcome a guest is to take them in, so the cricket body takes the letter inside
indicatorNotes.conclusion of: the conclusion of a word is its end, its last letter

annotation.surface: The cricket authority of old coolly greeting the end of a match.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In the past' looks like it sets the scene; it is a piece of wordplay, and the clue's pieces are ordered differently from the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Ice-cold, of a person, is figurative: so cool as to show no feeling at all.

entries.clue: Bloaters at sea giving up a seafood (7)

indicatorNotes.at sea: to be at sea is to be confused, so the letters are in disorder
indicatorNotes.giving up: to give something up is to surrender it, so the A leaves

blocks.note: BLOATERS with its A given up

annotation.surface: Smoked herrings abandoned in favour of other seafood.
annotation.walkthrough: A bloater is a whole smoked herring. 'At sea' suits the fishy surface while telling you to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: lobster is one kind of seafood.

entries.clue: Faithless lover is scared to move (8)

indicatorNotes.to move: letters that move leave their places, so the fodder is rearranged

annotation.surface: An unfaithful partner too frightened to budge.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface's scared figure never moves; the letters do. The answer is a literary character, not a word from the dictionary.
annotation.definitionFit: In Chaucer and Shakespeare, Cressida pledges herself to Troilus and then deserts him for Diomedes.

entries.clue: One with sense to restrict family of ill repute (8)

indicatorNotes.to restrict: to restrict something is to confine it, so NOUS closes around the family

blocks.note: FAMILY cut to its first three letters, the informal fam

annotation.surface: A sensible person keeping a disreputable family in check.
annotation.walkthrough: Nous is British slang for practical good sense. The surface ties 'of ill repute' to the family, but it stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Infamous means famous for the wrong reasons, which is having an ill repute.

entries.clue: Unreliable and profligate about spending, ultimately (5)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' means around, so the profligate goes around the letter
indicatorNotes.ultimately: ultimately means in the end, so take the final letter

blocks.note: a roué is a debauched man

annotation.surface: A description of a spendthrift who can't be trusted with money.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Profligate' looks like an adjective beside 'unreliable', but it is the noun, a roué. The adjective sense of rogue is the one in 'rogue trader'.
annotation.definitionFit: As an adjective, rogue means behaving erratically or out of control, so not to be relied on.

entries.clue: Bird’s prize for being first to reach summit (9)

blocks.note: the gold medal goes to the winner
the crest of a hill is its top

annotation.surface: A climbing race: the first to the top wins the prize.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bird’s prize' looks like a possessive, the bird's reward; the 's is 'is', leaving Bird as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the goldcrest is Europe's smallest bird, named for its yellow crown stripe.

entries.clue: Blade increasingly under soil (8)

indicatorNotes.under: in a down clue, one piece under another is written below it

annotation.surface: A blade of grass growing ever deeper under the soil.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blade' suggests grass beside the soil; it is a sword.
annotation.definitionFit: Blade stands for the whole weapon: a claymore is a large Scottish broadsword.

entries.clue: Greatly enjoy being ahead after part of race? (3,2)

indicatorNotes.after: 'after' means following, so UP comes after LAP

blocks.note: a lap is one circuit of a race
up = ahead, as in 'two goals up'

annotation.surface: A runner relishing a lead after one circuit.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all athletics, so 'greatly enjoy' reads as the runner's feeling rather than the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to lap up praise is to enjoy it eagerly, as a cat laps up cream.

entries.clue: Cartoon strip generating little money (7)

blocks.note: Charles Schulz's strip with Snoopy and Charlie Brown
the idiom for a trifling wage

annotation.surface: A comic strip that earns its creator next to nothing.
annotation.walkthrough: To be paid peanuts is to be paid very little. The irony is that the strip made Schulz a fortune.
annotation.definitionFit: One title, one idiom: Peanuts is the strip, and peanuts is slang for a tiny sum.

entries.clue: Shakespeare on demand, as it were: a lot of choice? (4,4)

blocks.note: the demand is a protest slogan calling for his release

annotation.surface: A campaign to release Shakespeare, framed as a matter of choice.
annotation.walkthrough: Picture a placard reading FREE WILL demanding the Bard's release. In the definition, 'lot' is one's lot in life: with free will your lot is your own choice.
annotation.definitionFit: Free will is the power to choose one's own course, so a lot, a fate, made of choice.

entries.clue: Heavy metal to damage stream after tipping (7)

indicatorNotes.after tipping: to tip something is to tilt it over, so in a down clue the letters end upside down

annotation.surface: Toxic metal fouling a stream after fly-tipping.
annotation.walkthrough: Tipping is British for dumping rubbish, which suits the polluted stream. 'Heavy metal' suggests rock music, but it is a chemical element.
annotation.definitionFit: Wolfram is the old name for tungsten, one of the densest metals.

entries.clue: Detectives turned up following obstruction of poet (6)

indicatorNotes.turned up: turned upward, so in a down clue the letters read from bottom to top
indicatorNotes.following: 'following' means coming after, so the detectives go after the bar

annotation.surface: Police arriving after someone obstructed a poet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' reads as the detectives arriving on the scene; it is the reversal. The CID is the British police's detective branch.
annotation.definitionFit: A bard is a poet, so bardic describes what belongs to one.

entries.clue: Cracked beam twisting round back of another part of mast (7)

indicatorNotes.twisting: to twist round is to turn back on yourself, so the string reads backwards
indicatorNotes.round: MAD goes round the R, holding it inside
indicatorNotes.back of: the back of a word is its end, its last letter

blocks.note: last letter of another, placed inside MAD as MRAD
a ray is a beam of light

annotation.surface: A split timber on a ship twisting around a mast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cracked beam' reads as one damaged spar, and a beam is ship's timber, but the words split in two.
annotation.definitionFit: The yardarm is the outer end of a yard, the spar that crosses the mast.

entries.clue: You are upset over protest excluding one from the country (5)

indicatorNotes.upset: to upset is to knock over, so in a down clue the letters flip
indicatorNotes.over: in a down clue, over means placed on top of what follows
indicatorNotes.excluding: to exclude is to leave out, so the letter for one goes

blocks.note: RAIL (to protest) without I, the Roman one

annotation.surface: An upset objector being expelled from the country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'From the country' reads as exile; it is the definition, meaning rustic.
annotation.definitionFit: Rural things come from the countryside rather than the town.

entries.clue: After distribution of fuel, account backed Nile vessel (7)

indicatorNotes.distribution of: distributing something scatters it about, so the letters are dealt out afresh
indicatorNotes.backed: backed means moved backwards, so the letters read in reverse

annotation.surface: Fuel shared out and the books balanced before a boat sets off on the Nile.
annotation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the rearranged fuel first; the account comes second and backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A felucca is the traditional wooden sailing boat still seen on the Nile, one vessel of that river.

entries.clue: Mount painting from book (5)

indicatorNotes.Mount: to mount is to climb, so in a down clue the letters go upwards

blocks.note: of = from, as in 'of noble birth'

annotation.surface: Mounting a picture taken from a book.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mount' looks like a picture mount, but is a verb telling you to go up.
annotation.definitionFit: A folio is a large book made of sheets folded once.

entries.clue: Novel form of uranium fluoride to expel iodine? About time (3,6,6)

indicatorNotes.form of: a new form of something is the same stuff reshaped, so the letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.to expel: to expel is to throw out, so the iodine's I leaves
indicatorNotes.About: 'about' means around, so the T joins the mix

blocks.note: I, the symbol for iodine, removed

annotation.surface: A chemistry recipe for a new uranium compound.
annotation.walkthrough: The chemistry is a front: 'Novel' looks like an adjective, a novel compound, but it is the definition, a book title.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Our Mutual Friend is Dickens's last completed novel.

entries.clue: Inclination to follow English North? Sign up (6)

indicatorNotes.to follow: to follow is to come after, so LIST comes after E and N

blocks.note: a ship's list is its lean

annotation.surface: A leaning towards heading north, then joining up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Inclination' suggests a wish; here it is a physical lean.
annotation.definitionFit: Enlisting is signing up for the armed forces, or for any cause.

entries.clue: Superficial company things backed by company’s leader (8)

indicatorNotes.backed: backed means moved backwards, so the letters read in reverse
indicatorNotes.leader: the leader goes first, so take the first letter of company

annotation.surface: A firm's shallow gestures, endorsed by its boss.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backed' reads as endorsed, a boss backing a plan; it reverses the things instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Cosmetic changes touch only the surface, like make-up on a face.
